w: What's tested Reading thyroid labs: primary (the gland) versus secondary (the pituitary) The pituitary's two lobes, its cells and hormones, its tumors and what happens when it fails ADH problems: diabetes insipidus and SIADH Too much thyroid (Graves), too little (Hashimoto, myxedema, cretinism) The five thyroid tumors: how each looks, its mutation and how it spreads The one rule to learn first Hormones run on feedback. The hypothalamus sends TRH, the pituitary sends TSH, the thyroid makes T3 and T4. When there is enough T4, it tells the pituitary to stop. So read T4 and TSH together. Opposite directions mean primary: the thyroid itself is the problem and feedback is working. Same direction means secondary: the pituitary is the problem. T4 high, TSH low: primary hyperthyroid (Graves). T4 high, TSH high: secondary hyperthyroid (a TSH-making pituitary tumor). T4 low, TSH high: primary hypothyroid (Hashimoto). T4 low, TSH low: secondary hypothyroid (a failed pituitary, like Sheehan). Dr. Dababneh called this "a typical question in anything." It works for every gland the pituitary controls. The pituitary It sits in the sella turcica, right under the optic chiasm. The front lobe is gland tissue. The back lobe is nerve fibers that store two hormones made in the hypothalamus. The front lobe has 5 cell types and 7 hormones. The name tells you the job: somatotrophs make growth hormone, mammotrophs make prolactin, corticotrophs make ACTH and MSH, thyrotrophs make TSH, gonadotrophs make FSH and LH. Dopamine is the brake on prolactin; somatostatin is the brake on growth hormone. Pituitary tumors Adenomas are now called PitNETs. Under 10 millimeters is a micro; over 10 is a macro. Big ones press on things: headache, nausea and vomiting, and loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopsia), because they squash the crossing fibers of the chiasm. Prolactinoma: the most common working tumor. No periods plus milk from the breasts. Usually small, in young women. Growth hormone: the biggest tumors. Child: gigantism. Adult: acromegaly (bigger skull and organs), plus high sugar, weak bones and high blood pressure. ACTH: Cushing disease. Moon face, belly fat, high sugar, high blood pressure. FSH and LH: no syndrome. Found because it is big. When the pituitary fails You have to lose about 75 percent of the front lobe first. Causes: a tumor that makes nothing (null cell), Sheehan syndrome (the gland dies from low blood pressure around childbirth), an empty sella, trauma, inflammation and cancer. Signs: tired, cold, low sex drive, no periods, can't breastfeed. ADH and oxytocin Oxytocin: labor contractions and milk let-down. No diseases to learn. ADH keeps water in through the kidney tubules and squeezes vessels. Diabetes insipidus: no ADH effect. Lots of watery urine, high sodium. Central means no ADH (head injury, surgery, tumors). Nephrogenic means the kidneys ignore normal ADH. It is not about sugar; "diabetes" just means lots of urine. SIADH: too much ADH. Water is kept, so sodium is low. The classic cause is small cell lung cancer. The thyroid It starts at the back of the tongue and moves down to the neck. If it stops early, you get a lingual thyroid at the base of the tongue; a leftover duct gives a thyroglossal duct cyst. Follicular cells make T3 and T4. C cells make calcitonin, which acts on bone. Goiter means a big thyroid; iodine deficiency is the usual cause. Too much thyroid Everything speeds up: weight loss, fast or irregular heart, tremor, nerves, sweating, heat intolerance, diarrhea. Graves is the most common cause: an antibody turns ON the TSH receptor. Whole-gland enlargement, bulging eyes, mostly women (5 to 1). Too little thyroid Everything slows down: weight gain, cold, tired, slow thinking, coarse face, puffy hands and a big tongue (myxedema). In a child it is cretinism: short, slow development, big head, big tongue. Hashimoto is the most common cause in the US: lymphocytes fill the gland, and as taught, the antibody turns OFF the TSH receptor. Graves turns it on, Hashimoto turns it off. Thyroid tumors Follicular adenoma: benign, one painless cold nodule, wrapped in an intact capsule. Follicular carcinoma: breaks through its capsule or into blood vessels. Spreads by blood to lung and bone. RAS. Women around 50. Removing one lobe is enough. Papillary carcinoma: the most common (60 to 80 percent). Young, radiation. Spreads by lymph to neck nodes. BRAF. Can be in several spots, so the whole gland comes out. Pale "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies (calcified dead papillae) in half. Over 80 percent alive at 10 years. Medullary carcinoma: from C cells. RET, MEN 2. Makes amyloid. Stains for calcitonin, chromogranin and CEA. Familial cases are younger and in both lobes. Anaplastic carcinoma: old patients (60 to 80), goiter areas, a neck mass that grows in weeks and kills fast. Looks like nothing. Rush it for mutation testing. Memory hook: Follicular travels Far, by blood to lung and bone; Papillary stays Put, in the neck nodes by lymph. BRAF for papillary, RAS for follicular, RET for medullary. What a dentist might notice A lump at the base of the tongue in the midline: think lingual thyroid, tissue that never moved down. A big tongue, a coarse face and puffy hands: think hypothyroidism (myxedema), or cretinism in a child. A racing, irregular pulse, tremor, sweating and nerves in the chair: think hyperthyroidism, often Graves. An adult whose skull and head keep getting bigger: think acromegaly from a growth hormone tumor. Easy mix-ups Gigantism is a child; acromegaly is an adult. Graves turns the TSH receptor on; Hashimoto, as taught, turns it off. Diabetes insipidus: high sodium, watery urine. SIADH: low sodium. Follicular adenoma vs carcinoma: only invasion of the capsule or a vessel tells them apart. Papillary nuclei are pale, not dark. Psammoma bodies mean papillary; amyloid means medullary. Follicular carcinoma: take one lobe. Papillary: take the whole gland, because it can be in more than one spot. Prolactinoma makes milk; Sheehan syndrome stops it.
